summary: This work presents a multi-stage Mamba-based qubit state discriminator for superconducting quantum processors that achieves 0.906–0.911 geometric-mean readout fidelity while reducing model parameters by 49.6–99.4% compared to prior state-of-the-art approaches. The architecture integrates sequence modeling via a structured state machine for initial state discrimination with a neural error detector for post-correcting relaxation-induced errors, maintaining 0.893 fidelity at 500 ns readout durations and enabling 26% reduction in surface-code logical error rate relative to existing methods.
motivation: Readout is the most error-prone and latency-critical stage in superconducting quantum computers, with measurement errors 12× higher than gate errors and durations 23–38× longer than two-qubit gates, severely limiting mid-circuit measurement feedback required for quantum error correction. Frequency-multiplexed architectures introduce additional crosstalk-induced errors, while existing feed-forward neural network discriminators suffer from parameter counts scaling multiplicatively with trace length, hindering scalability to multi-qubit systems.
method: The authors employ Mamba, a state-space model with linear computational complexity, to replace fully connected layers in the discriminator, decoupling model size from readout trace length. A two-stage pipeline uses a Mamba classifier for initial state discrimination, followed by a second Mamba-based error detector trained on hard-to-classify relaxation events using focal loss, with optional incorporation of helper traces from neighboring qubits identified via conditional error probability analysis to mitigate localized crosstalk.
result: The lightweight single-qubit model achieves $F_{5Q} = 0.906$ with 769 parameters per qubit on 1.6 million experimental multiplexed traces from a five-qubit superconducting processor, while the optimal variant with helper traces and detector reaches $F_{5Q} = 0.911$; both maintain $F_{5Q} \geq 0.893$ at 500 ns duration, compared to $\sim 0.89$ for prior methods at 700 ns, enabling up to 26% lower logical error rate in surface-code simulations under IBM Heron noise assumptions.
